outputs.L1:
**The Golden Water-Lily**

O summer water-lily! when the brook is gliding
So slow and smooth adown its sedgy bed,
Upon thy broad leaves so safely riding
The water's surface with thy yellow head,
By alder shades, O,
And bulrush beds, O,
Thou then dost float, O golden summer lily!

The grey-boughed willow leans down lowly
Above the water thy leaves do hide;
The bending bulrush, swaying slowly,
Doth skirt in summer thy river's side;
And perch in shoals, O,
Do fill the holes, O,
Where thou dost float, O golden summer lily!

Oh! when thy brook-drinking flower is blowing,
The burning summer is setting in;
The time of greenness, the time of mowing,
When in the hay-field, with sunburnt skin,
The folk do drink, O,
Upon the brink, O,
Where thou dost float, O golden summer lily!

With arms outspreading, and cheeks a-blowing,
How proud was I when I first could swim
Athwart the deep place where thou art growing,
With thy long root from the bottom dim;
While cows, knee-high, O,
In brook, were nigh, O,
Where thou dost float, O golden summer lily!

Of all the brooks through the meads a-winding,
Of all the meads by a river's brim,
There's none so fair of my own heart's finding
As where the maidens do see thee swim,
And stand to take, O,
With long-stemmed rake, O,
Thy flower afloat, O golden summer lily!
outputs.L2:
**The Golden Summer Water-Lily**

Oh golden lily of the summer! When the stream slips by so gently and smoothly along its reedy channel, your yellow blossom rides safely atop the water on your wide leaves. Beside the shadows of the alder trees and the clusters of bulrushes, there you drift, golden summer lily!

The willow with its grey branches bends down low over the water where your leaves are concealed; the curving bulrush, gently rocking back and forth, borders the edge of your river throughout the summer. And schools of perch crowd into the deep hollows where you float, golden summer lily!

Ah, when your flower that sips from the brook comes into bloom, the scorching summer is arriving; it's the season of lush green and of haymaking, when out in the hayfield the people—their skin browned by the sun—stop to drink at the water's edge, right where you float, golden summer lily!

With my arms stretched wide and my cheeks puffed out, how proud I felt the first time I managed to swim across the deep spot where you grow, your long root trailing up from the murky bottom. Meanwhile the cows stood nearby, wading knee-deep in the stream, close to where you float, golden summer lily!

Of every brook that twists its way through the meadows, and of every meadow lying along a riverbank, none seems as lovely to my own heart as the one where the young women come to watch you drift, and pause to gather your floating bloom with their long-handled rakes, golden summer lily!

# The Golden Summer Water-Lily

Upon the smooth and slow-moving brook, the golden summer water-lily—the zummer clote—floats gently, cradled amid the cool shade of alders and the sheltering beds of bulrush. Here the water drifts with unhurried ease, and the bright bloom rests upon its surface like a small sun set adrift among the shadows.

The riverside itself is a scene of quiet abundance. Grey willows lean low toward the water, their branches trailing above the current, while the tall bulrushes sway with every passing breeze. Beneath the surface, shoals of perch crowd the deep holes and hollows where the flower makes its home, filling those still waters with silent, darting life.

When the water-lily opens its golden bloom, it heralds the coming of high summer—that rich season of greenness, of mowing and haymaking, when the sunburnt labourers pause in their toil to drink beside the brink of the stream. The flower is thus a marker of the year's fullest and warmest days.

The sight of it stirs a memory in the speaker, who recalls with fondness the pride he felt as a boy. It was here, in the deep place where the flower grew, that he first learned to swim, striking out across the water while the cows stood knee-deep along the margins, calmly grazing near the bank.

Yet among all the brooks and meadows he has known, it is this one place the speaker holds most dear. For here the maidens come to gather at the water's edge, leaning out over the current to reach and take the floating flower for their own. It is this gentle scene, above all others, that binds his heart forever to this small and treasured stretch of stream.
outputs.L4:
# The Zummer Clote

Along the meandering course of a slow country brook, where the water moves with unhurried patience through the heart of the Dorset countryside, there floats a flower of quiet golden splendour—the zummer clote, the summer water-lily, whose broad leaves rest upon the surface like small islands of green. This humble bloom, so easily overlooked by the hurried traveller, becomes in the speaker's affectionate eyes a thing of genuine wonder, deserving of celebration in the warm, rounded tones of rustic Dorset speech.

Here the alders lean over the water's edge, their branches trailing toward the current, while tall bulrushes stand like sentinels among the reeds. The brook winds past meadows where the haymaking is underway, and the air carries the sweet scent of cut grass and the distant sounds of labourers at their seasonal work. Everywhere the eye turns, the ordinary rhythms of rural life unfold: cattle wading at the shallows to drink, birds darting low across the shining water, and the gentle stir of summer breezes moving through the long grass along the banks.

As the seasons turn, the poem lingers over vivid scenes that mark the passing year, each one bound to the brook and its faithful golden flower. Yet it is not the landscape alone that stirs the speaker's heart. Memory rises unbidden—recollections of boyhood days when he swam in these same waters, when the brook was a place of freedom and delight, and the clote floated just as it does now, unchanged by all the years between. These personal remembrances give the pastoral scene a deeper resonance, weaving the beauty of the present moment together with the tender ache of the past.

And so, having wandered in thought along its banks and among its memories, the speaker arrives at his heartfelt declaration: that this flower-adorned brook, with its floating golden clote, is the fairest of them all. In this simple pronouncement lies something larger—a celebration of the enduring beauty of the natural countryside and the profound emotional significance it holds. The zummer clote becomes more than a flower; it is a symbol of home, of memory, and of the quiet, abiding loveliness of the rural world that shaped the speaker's very soul.
outputs.L5:
# The Weight of Ancient Words

**Upon** the crumbling pages of forgotten manuscripts, we discover words that carry the whispers of centuries past. Language, ever-shifting like sand beneath the tide, once wore a different garment—more formal, more reverent, and yet somehow more intimate.

Consider the humble word **"the."** Though it seems ordinary, appearing thousands of times in our daily speech, it serves as the quiet foundation upon which entire sentences are built. Without it, our language would collapse into fragments, losing the specificity and clarity we so often take for granted. It points, it defines, it separates the particular from the general.

Then there is **"thou,"** a word that has slipped away from common usage, surviving only in poetry, scripture, and the dusty corners of literature. Once, "thou" was the mark of closeness—reserved for friends, family, and lovers—while "you" carried a measure of distance and respect. How strange that a word once so tender now sounds so grand and ceremonial to modern ears.

**Upon** reflection, these three small words reveal how deeply language shapes our understanding of the world. Each one carries history within its letters. When we read "Thou shalt not" or "Upon this rock," we feel the gravity of tradition pressing against our present moment.

Perhaps the beauty of such words lies not in their frequency, but in their power to connect us—across time, across cultures, across the vast silence that separates the living from those who spoke before us.

counterfactuals.output:
William Barnes (1801–1886) was a Dorset poet and philologist who wrote extensively in the Dorset dialect. His work is now in the public domain, so I can share a complete poem with you.

Here's "My Orcha'd in Linden Lea," one of his best-known poems (later set to music by Ralph Vaughan Williams):

**My Orcha'd in Linden Lea**

'Ithin the woodlands, flow'ry gleaded,
By the woak tree's mossy moot,
The sheenen grass-bleades, timber-shaded,
Now do quiver under voot;
An' birds do whissle over head,
An' water's bubblen in its bed,
An' there vor me the apple tree
Do lean down low in Linden Lea.

When leaves that leately were a-springen
Now do feade 'ithin the copse,
An' painted birds do hush their zingen
Up upon the timber's tops;
An' brown-leav'd fruit's a-turnen red,
In cloudless zunsheen, over head,
Wi' fruit vor me, the apple tree
Do lean down low in Linden Lea.

Let other vo'k meake money vaster
In the air o' dark-room'd towns,
I don't dread a peevish measter;
Though noo man do heed my frowns,
I be free to goo abrode,
Or teake ageän my hwomeward road
To where, vor me, the apple tree
Do lean down low in Linden Lea.

This poem nicely illustrates several features of the Dorset dialect that Barnes tried to capture phonetically:
- The **"z"** for "s" sounds (*zingen*, *zunsheen*) — a voicing typical of southwest English
- The **"v"** for "f" (*voot*, *vor*, *vo'k*) — another West Country voicing feature
- The **"w"** intrusion in words like *woak* (oak) and *hwomeward* (homeward)
- The **"-en"** verb endings (*bubblen*, *springen*, *zingen*)
- The prefix **"a-"** on participles (*a-springen*, *a-turnen*)

Barnes was deliberate about these spellings because he was a trained philologist who saw the Dorset dialect as a purer descendant of Anglo-Saxon than standard English. If you're studying his work, his collection *Poems of Rural Life in the Dorset Dialect* (1844) would be a great primary source.
